title: LIRC Unemployment Insurance Decision — Weiss1
text:
STATE OF WISCONSIN CIRCUIT COURT COLUMBii COUNTY
----------------------------------------------------------------
TIMOTHY WEISS; DECISION AND ORDER
Plaintiff, Case 98CV050
v.
LABOR AND INDUSTRY REVIEW COMMISSION,
THE BRUCE COMPANY OF WISCONSIN, INC., and
GTE NORTH INC. , c / o GATES MCDONALD CO. ,
I
Defendants.
-~-------------------------------------------
This is an action to review decisions of the Labor and
Industry Re-view Commission respecting unemployment compensation
benefits of the Plaintiff, Timothy J. Weiss. The sole issue
raised by the Plaintiff is that the procedure followed before the
administrative law judge violated his rights to·due process.
The· scope of judicial review in this matter is set forth in
Section 102.23(1) Wis. Stats~ The bases ~or setting aside a
commission determination are limited t.o the·. following: .
"1. That the commission acted without or in eXC$SS of
its powers.
2. That the order or award was procured by fraud.
3 . That the findings of fact by the co:rhnd: s s i_on do not
support the order or award."
The scope of judicial review has been addressed in a
multitude of cases. It is sufficient for the purposes of this
case to note that no issue of fraud is raised nor is there any
issue respecting the sufficiency of the evidence to sup~ort the
findings of the Commission. ·The sole issue is whether there was
a due process violation sufficient 'to warrant relief to the
1

Plaintiff.
A brief was filed by the Plaintiff, a response brief was
filed by the commission, and a reply brief was filed by the
Plaintiff. I have reviewed the hearing record, eacJ:i: of the
briefs filed by the parties, and the -cases cited in each brief.
It should first be noted that the Plaintiff does not argue
that there is any question regarding the honesty or integrity of
the administrative law judge. Although Plaintiff's initial brief
implies some bias on the part of the administrative law judge,
Plaintiff's reply brief removes that issue from contention.
There is no dispute that the hearings before the
administrative law judge were attended only by the judge, the
Plaintiff and Plaintiff's counsel .. During the course of the
hearings, the administrative law judge questioned the Plaintiff
and initiated receipt of exhibits as part of the record.
Plaintiff argues, by reason of this conduct, that the
administrative law judge "assumed the role of prosecutor."
Plaintiff asserts that the "prosecutorial" role is
demonstrated by the following:
1. ·"c·lassical cross-examination techniques,'.' including
leading questions
2. attacking uncontradicted statements
3. tone of voice and body language
4. disparate application of evidentiary rules and receipt
of exhibits into the record
5. representing the department
I note that it is not possible to address the issue of the
tone of voice and body language used by the administrative law
judge. This is a review of the record only, and the record does
2

not reveal. anything regarding those matters.
Plaintiff cites three Wisconsin cases in support of his
argument that the procedure followed here violated due process.
They are State ex rel. Ball v. McPhee, 6 Wis.2d 190 (1959),
Guthrie v. Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission,
111 Wis.2d 447 (1983), and Nova Services, Inc. v. Village of
Saukville, 211 Wis. 2d 690 (ct. App. 1997). The Defendant argues
that the administrative law judge simply carried out the
necessary and expected function of a hearing officer. It argues
that Plaintiff makes a thinly veiled claim that the
administrative law judge was biased against him.
Defendant argues that the administrative law judge was
investigatorial rather than prosecutorial. It argues that there
is a distinction between a prosecutor, whci has the responsibility
of obtaining a particular result, and an investigator, who
pursues relevant evidence in an attempt to arrive at a result
dictated by the evidence. Defendant does not cite published
cases in response to the allegation that the administrative law
judge acted in a prosecutorial manner. However, it does cite the
provisions o.f' Section 108. 09 ( 5) ( a) ·wis. stats. , which provides
that hearings shall be conducted pursuant to department rules.
Also cited are the provisions of Chapter DWD, section 140.15 Wis.
Administrative Code which provides, in part, as follows:
11 (2) The Administrative Law Judge has the
responsibility to develop the facts and may call and
examine any witness that he or she deems necessary ... "
The cases cited by the Plaintiff can be distinguished from
3

this case. In each of the cases cited by the Plaintiff, there
was a responsibility of the participant to represent the
interests of a party. Here, the administrative law judge did not
have the responsibility to represent the Defendants.
The concern expressed by the Plaintiff is not without some
substance. However, the administrative law judge is charged with
the responsibility of developing a record. That is of particular
importance here, where the law provides for more than one level
of review. The initial action is appealable to the hearing
examiner and that decision, based upon the record,· is reviewable
by the Commission.
My review of this record leads to the conclusion that there
was no violation of the Plaintiff's rights to due process. The
Plaintiff disavows any allegation of·bias and acknowledges the
presumption of honesty and integrity on the part of adjudicators
in administrative proceedings, State ex rel, DeLuca v. common
council, 72 Wis.2d 672 (1976). To the extent that there is an
implication of bias in Plaintiff's original argument, I find that
none is shown in the record. Furthermore, the rulings made by
the administrative ·1a.;r judge respecting the a.dmission of exhibits
into the record did not result in a denial of due process.
Situations in which one party is not represented by counsel
creates some difficulty for a hearing examiner, similar to the
difficulty that can occur when prose litigants appear before
courts. It would be best if all parties were represented by
counsel who thoroughly develop a record in matters of this type.
4

.
'
However, when one party is not represented or present, the ends
of justice require that the adjudicator have available the
information necessary to make a reasoned determination. I cannot
conclude that the mere poss°ibility of some abuse occurring as a
result of the active participation of the administrative law.
judge in developing the record translates into a violation of due
process.
ORDER.
Based upon the foregoing, the relief requested by the
Plaintiff is hereby denied and the decision of the commission is
affirmed.
Dated this 8th day of December, 1998.
BY THE COURT:
HoIn . ~R.i chard L. Rehm•
Circuit Judge
